caption: For unit vectors the dot product is the length of b's shadow on a: 0.866 at 30 degrees passes the 0.707 cone test, 0.5 at 60 degrees fails, 0 is perpendicular and -1 is opposite.
Same rotation, same translation, different order: rotate-then-translate turns the square in place at its new spot, translate-then-rotate swings it around the origin.
As pitch reaches 90 degrees the roll axis swings onto the yaw axis, so two Euler angles now spin the object the same way and one degree of freedom is gone.
Follow one head vertex through every space: the model, view and projection matrices, then the fixed divide by w and the viewport map it to a pixel (camera at (10, 1.2, 0), 60 degree FOV, 16:9).
The projection copies depth into w, so dividing by it shrinks an object in proportion to its distance: the same bar at 2.7 times the depth is 1/2.7 as tall on screen.
With standard 24-bit depth the smallest resolvable gap grows with distance squared, reaching 0.15 m at 500 m; reversed-Z with a float32 buffer keeps it orders of magnitude smaller across the range.
Only the vertex and fragment stages run your code; everything between them, including clipping, rasterization and the depth test, is fixed-function hardware.
The rasterizer tests pixel centres, but shading runs in 2x2 quads: every quad the triangle touches launches four lanes, so edge pixels and tiny triangles pay for helper lanes that produce nothing.
Pipelined, a 6 ms CPU and a 14 ms GPU deliver a frame every 14 ms; a blocking readback forces them to take turns and every frame costs 6 + 14 = 20 ms.
Every fragment gets a barycentric blend of its three vertices' outputs; blending two unit normals gives a shorter vector, which is why the fragment shader re-normalizes.
When lanes disagree on a branch the warp runs both sides with lanes masked off and pays shadeA plus shadeB; a coherent warp pays for one side only.

Each independent on/off keyword doubles the compiled programs: 10 keywords make 2^10 = 1,024 variants for one pass, while the worked example drops from 288 to 36 by moving three features to uniform branches.
